Zdunska Wola Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Zduńska Wola, Poland

Not demolished. NOTE: the source page's address, coordinates, and city fields for this record were found to be duplicated from the unrelated Łask New Jewish Cemetery entry, so those specific fields are not used here; the coordinates above are an approximate town-center location for Zduńska Wola, not the precise cemetery site. The narrative below, however, is Zduńska Wola-specific and appears reliable. Zduńska Wola, first recorded around 1394 and granted town rights only in 1825, saw its first documented Jewish residents in 1788; a formal community organized in 1828, including Jews from surrounding villages, and grew to 5,983 (of 20,472 total residents) by 1902. Germans established a ghetto in spring 1940, holding 8,300 people by December that year; its August 1942 liquidation sent most residents to Chełmno, with skilled craftsmen transferred to the Łódź Ghetto and 150 people shot on the spot. This cemetery was established around 1826, with its oldest surviving tombstone dated 1832 and its last burial in 1964. Germans destroyed it during WWII; a notably rare feature among Polish Jewish cemeteries is its inclusion of matzevot made from erratic boulders alongside more typical granite, limestone, and sandstone stones. A 1994 monument honors victims from the ghetto's liquidation, buried in a mass grave here. In 2001, the grounds were formally re-divided into 11 documentation plots (not reflecting the original historic layout), and a 2007 replica gate was installed with a multilingual historical plaque. The site is now maintained by the YACHAD Historical Society, former Zduńska Wola residents now in Israel, local authorities, and the city history museum, with annual open days since 2010.
